title: JMA Wireless Lean Six Sigma Lead
summary_easy: From January to May 2026, Tanay led a four person Lean Six Sigma team at JMA Wireless, a cell tower equipment maker, in the department that builds jumper cables. The team got five performance measures defined the same way for a manual line and an automated cell, built the data pipeline and dashboard, and found that the automated cell was almost never broken but was starved of parts. A daily standup Tanay piloted cut the time to act on a red measure from about four hours to about 25 minutes, and the projected value is about $355,000 a year pending the company's finance team.
summary_deep: A 15 week DMAIC engagement sponsored by JMA's SVP of Global Operations. In Define, Tanay ran definition interviews across manufacturing, quality, and production supervision and wrote a sponsor approved document fixing one formula and one target for Parts per Labor Hour, Uptime, First Time Throughput, Schedule Attainment, and a Culture and Engagement index. In Measure, a pandas and openpyxl pipeline walked the automated cell's three level nested PLC JSON with explicit json_normalize record paths to one typed row per test event with derived cycle time, taking data that expanded past 31 GB in Power BI down to under 5 MB. The standardized baseline showed the automated cell at 97.3% uptime but 46.3% schedule attainment, an input limited pattern that a fishbone traced to kitting batched for the manual line, batched connector subassemblies, and a commissioning era target, while the manual line masked the gap at 139.7%. Improve chose three fixes from six with a Pugh matrix (daily dashboard standup, two bin kitting, a target reset to about 1,150 cables a week with a ramp), and a two week standup pilot cut median red to first action from about 4 hours to about 25 minutes. Control delivered a Control Plan with a refresh owner, a dashboard FMEA, and tiered escalation. The roughly $355,000 a year is a projection on conservative assumed rates pending JMA Finance; the stated gaps are no pipeline unit tests and no culture baseline.

sheet.easy:
## What it was
- **JMA Wireless**, Liverpool NY: cell tower transmitters and 5G infrastructure. Client engagement, Jan to May 2026 (ended).
- Tanay was **Project Lead** of a four person Whitman School team, 15 weeks, on site weekly, sponsored by the **SVP of Global Operations** with a named project champion. Counted toward the Lean Six Sigma Green Belt (SCM 755).
- Department: **Jumper** cables. Jumper 1.0 is manual (eight operators, two ten hour shifts). Jumper 2.0 is a fully automated cell.

## The problem
Nobody could compare the two lines, because words like Uptime meant different things to different teams.

## What Tanay did (DMAIC)
| Phase | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Define | Charter, SIPOC, CTQC tree, interviews; five KPIs with one formula and one target each, sponsor approved |
| Measure | Python pipeline: 31 GB of nested machine JSON (as expanded in Power BI) to under 5 MB |
| Analyze | 97.3% uptime but 46.3% of target on the automated cell; fishbone and two Paretos |
| Improve | Six ideas, Pugh matrix, three picks; daily standup piloted |
| Control | Control Plan: refresh owner, dashboard FMEA, escalation on red |

## The five KPIs
| KPI | Formula | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parts per Labor Hour | good parts / labor hours | at least 50 |
| Uptime | runtime / (runtime + downtime) | at least 85% |
| First Time Throughput | good parts / parts tested | at least 95% |
| Schedule Attainment | actual parts / weekly target | at least 100% |
| Culture and Engagement | pulse 60% + weekly active dashboard users 40% | index at least 75 |

## The finding
The automated cell was almost never down yet built less than half its target, so it was **starved**: the constraint was kitting and material flow upstream. The manual line hid this by running at 139.7% of its own target.

## Results
- Pilot: red KPI to first action, about 4 hours to about 25 minutes; KPI familiarity 2.4 to 4.1 out of 5.
- About **$355K a year projected** (27,000 cables at an assumed $12 margin plus 48 analyst hours a week at an assumed $12.50), pending JMA Finance.

## Honest limits
- Pilot was two weeks on one shift. Culture KPI has no baseline. No unit tests on the pipeline.
sheet.deep:
## Engagement facts
- JMA Wireless Jumper Department, Liverpool NY. Jan to May 2026, 15 weeks, weekly on site. Four person Whitman team; Tanay Project Lead. Sponsor: SVP of Global Operations; named project champion. Lean Six Sigma Green Belt, SCM 755, Spring 2026.
- Tanay owned: charter, SIPOC, CTQC tree, KPI definition interviews, Python pipeline, Control Plan; ran the standup pilot.
- Lines: Jumper 1.0 manual, eight operators, two ten hour shifts. Jumper 2.0 fully automated cell with PLC level data capture. Tests per cable: continuity, return loss, visual.
- Tools: Python, pandas, openpyxl, Power BI, DAX, Minitab, SIPOC, Pugh matrix, FMEA, Control Plan.

## KPI definitions (sponsor approved)
$$\text{PPLH}=\frac{\text{good parts}}{\text{labor hours}}\ (\ge 50)\qquad \text{Uptime}=\frac{\text{runtime}}{\text{runtime}+\text{downtime}}\ (\ge 85\%)$$
$$\text{FTT}=\frac{\text{good parts}}{\text{parts tested}}\ (\ge 95\%)\qquad \text{SA}=\frac{\text{actual parts}}{\text{weekly target}}\ (\ge 100\%)$$
$$\text{C\&E}=0.6\cdot\text{pulse}+0.4\cdot\text{weekly active dashboard users}\ (\ge 75)$$
- Pulse: five questions, two minutes. Usage: distinct named users opening the dashboard at least twice a week. Scaling of both parts to 0 to 100 must be stated.
- PPLH trap: same scheduled labor hours denominator on both lines; automated cell needs a technician for part of a shift, so on engaged technician minutes it is roughly an order of magnitude higher; dashboard also shows cycles per engaged hour.

## Data pipeline
| Stage | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Extract | load raw test report JSON (record, then tests, then measurements, then channel readings) |
| Parse | `pd.json_normalize` with explicit `record_path`, `meta` for parent fields |
| Type cast | datetime64, float64, boolean |
| Calculate | cycle time in seconds from start and end timestamps |
| Load | Power BI ready workbook via openpyxl |
- Input: two raw datasets of 809 and 1,000 records, more than 31 GB when expanded in Power BI; unopenable below 64 GB RAM. Output: under 5 MB, instant refresh.
- Row explosion: rows $= \sum_{\text{records}} T \cdot M \cdot C$, each repeating parent columns; sibling arrays expanded independently create cross products.
- DAX pattern: `Uptime = DIVIDE(SUM(runtime), SUM(runtime) + SUM(downtime))`.

## Baseline (standardized definitions)
| KPI | Jumper 1.0 | Jumper 2.0 | Target |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FTT | 87.9% | 92.5% | 95% |
| Uptime | 31.3% | 97.3% | 85% |
| Schedule Attainment | 139.7% | 46.3% | 100% |
| PPLH | 34.9 | 7.94 | 50 |

## Analyze
- Finding: 97.3% uptime with 46.3% attainment means input limited. Manual line at 139.7% absorbed the shortfall and masked the demand signal.
- Fishbone leading causes: Method (kitting batches sized for the manual line), Material (connector subassemblies batched), Measurement (commissioning era weekly target never revisited).
- Quality Pareto (Jumper 1.0): torque and return loss 74% of first time failures.
- Downtime Pareto (Jumper 1.0): material wait 38% (18 min, about 24 a week), setup and changeover 27% (32 min, about 9), tool calibration and maintenance 19% (22 min, about 9), operator absent or break overrun 12% (11 min, about 11), other 4%. Shares sum to 100%, so they are shares of downtime; duration times frequency (about 17 hours a week) does not reconcile to 31.3% uptime by itself.
- Loops: a root cause failed validation and went back for re analysis; an unreachable target was revalidated.
- Theory of constraints: identify, exploit, subordinate, raise capacity, repeat. Drum buffer rope. Here the constraint was a policy and method constraint in kitting.
- OEE check: OEE = Availability x Performance x Quality, and starved time is an availability loss; know how cell states were classified.

## Improve
- Six candidates, Pugh matrix, benefit and effort grid. Picks: 15 minute daily standup at a wall mounted dashboard screen; two bin continuous kitting feed; target reset to roughly 1,150 cables a week with a ramp of about 200 a week.
- Pilot (two weeks, manual line first shift): median red to first action about 4 h to about 25 min; KPI familiarity 2.4 to 4.1 of 5 (self reported). No control group.

## Control
- Control Plan: named refresh owner and cadence; dashboard FMEA ($\text{RPN}=S\times O\times D$); tiered escalation on red.

## Business case (projection)
$$27{,}000 \times \$12 \approx \$324{,}000 \qquad 48 \times 52 \times \$12.50 = \$31{,}200 \qquad \text{total} \approx \$355{,}000$$
- Conservative assumed rates in an assumptions table, pending JMA Finance. Cable recovery projected from demonstrated capability.

## Validation and testing
- Definitions validated by sponsor sign off before build. Root causes validated with data (one failed). Pilot measured. No unit tests on the pipeline (stated gap).

## Limitations and scale
- Script plus workbook; no tests; no governed metric layer; culture KPI without baseline; small pilot; projection only.
- At 10x: warehouse table partitioned by date and line, incremental loads keyed on test event id, schema validation at ingest, orchestration, one governed KPI layer (dbt or shared semantic model).

## Next
- Implement two bin kitting and track attainment against the ramp; first culture survey; staggered standup rollout to second shift; Finance confirmation of rates; pipeline assertions; explicit starved time measure.

narration.script:
JMA Wireless builds cell tower equipment in Liverpool, New York. From January to May 2026 I led a four person Whitman team through a full DMAIC engagement in their Jumper Department, sponsored by the SVP of Global Operations, with a named champion and weekly on site access.

The department runs two lines side by side: a manual line with eight operators across two ten hour shifts, and a fully automated cell. Nobody could compare them, because Uptime and Schedule Attainment meant different things to different functions. In Define I ran interviews across manufacturing, quality, and production supervision and wrote a definition document with one formula and one target for five KPIs: Parts per Labor Hour, Uptime, First Time Throughput, Schedule Attainment, and a Culture and Engagement index. The sponsor approved it before we built anything.

Then the data. The automated cell writes one JSON record per test event, with three levels of arrays inside. Two small raw datasets expanded past 31 GB in Power BI. I flattened them in pandas with explicit json_normalize record paths to one row per test event, cast the types in Python, derived cycle time, and wrote a workbook under 5 MB.

The finding came from the definitions. The automated cell showed 97.3% uptime and 46.3% of its weekly target. A cell that's almost always up but misses plan by half is input limited, so the constraint was kitting and material flow upstream, and the manual line was hiding it by running at 139.7% of its own target.

We picked three fixes out of six with a Pugh matrix: a daily standup at a dashboard screen, a two bin kitting feed, and a target reset with a ramp. I piloted the standup for two weeks, and median time from red to first action fell from about four hours to about 25 minutes. The projected opportunity is about $355,000 a year, pending JMA Finance. What I'd change: I never wrote unit tests for the pipeline, and the culture metric never got a baseline.

Pipeline: nested JSON, 31 GB to under 5 MB

narration.prompt: Give me the full story, as you would to a senior engineer.
narration.script:
I'll give you the whole engagement, including the parts that were hard.

JMA Wireless's Jumper Department builds RF jumper cables, and every cable has to pass continuity, return loss, and visual inspection. Jumper 1.0 is manual, eight operators over two ten hour shifts. Jumper 2.0 is a fully automated cell with PLC level data capture. I led a four person team for fifteen weeks, sponsored by the SVP of Global Operations, with a project champion and weekly on site access.

Define was the most important phase. I wrote the charter, the SIPOC, and the CTQC tree, and ran KPI definition interviews across manufacturing, quality, and production supervision. Uptime and Schedule Attainment meant different things to different functions, so leadership couldn't connect the floor to the financial plan. The output was a sponsor approved document with one formula and one target per KPI. Parts per Labor Hour is good parts over labor hours, target 50. Uptime is runtime over runtime plus downtime, target 85%. First Time Throughput is good parts over parts tested, target 95%. Schedule Attainment is actual parts over weekly target, target 100%. Culture and Engagement weights a five question pulse survey at 60% and weekly active dashboard users at 40%, target 75.

Measure was a data engineering problem. The cell publishes one JSON record per test event; each record nests tests, each test nests measurements, each measurement nests channel readings. Two raw datasets of 809 and 1,000 records expanded past 31 GB in Power BI, because Power BI expanded the nesting on every visual, and nobody under 64 GB of RAM could open the file. I wrote a pandas and openpyxl pipeline that walks the nesting with explicit json_normalize record paths and writes one flat row per test event. It casts timestamps to datetime, readings to float, and pass or fail to boolean, so Power Query never coerces anything, and it derives cycle time in seconds for the Uptime and labor productivity measures. The output is under 5 MB and refreshes instantly.

Analyze is where the definitions paid off. On the standardized baseline the automated cell showed 97.3% uptime and 46.3% schedule attainment. Those can't both describe a machine problem. A cell that's up almost all the time and misses plan by more than half is input limited. The manual line was absorbing the shortfall at 139.7% of its own target, which looks heroic but masks the demand signal to planning. A fishbone on the gap put the leading causes in Method, Material, and Measurement: kitting batches sized for the manual line, connector subassemblies arriving in batches, and a weekly target set at commissioning and never revisited. Two Paretos backed it: torque and return loss were 74% of first time failures on the manual line, and material wait was the largest downtime category at 38%. One candidate root cause failed validation and went back for re analysis.

Improve: six candidates, a Pugh matrix, and a benefit and effort grid gave three recommendations: a fifteen minute daily standup at a wall mounted dashboard screen, a two bin continuous kitting feed, and a reset of the cell's target to demonstrated capability, roughly 1,150 cables a week, with a ramp of about 200 a week as kitting improves. I piloted the standup for two weeks on first shift. Median time from a KPI going red to a named owner acting fell from about four hours to about 25 minutes, and self reported KPI familiarity went from 2.4 to 4.1 out of five.

Control: a Control Plan with a named refresh owner and cadence, an FMEA on the dashboard itself, and tiered escalation on red status.

The money is a projection. About 27,000 recoverable cables a year at an assumed $12 margin is about $324,000, plus about 48 analyst hours a week at an assumed $12.50 is about $31,200, so about $355,000, pending JMA Finance.

What I'd challenge myself on: the pilot is one shift for two weeks with no control group. Uptime alone can't separate starved time from slow cycles, so I'd add starved time as its own measure. The culture KPI has no baseline. And the pipeline has no unit tests, so an upstream schema change would only be caught by someone noticing a wrong dashboard.

narration.prompt: If the cell was starved, that idle time should count as downtime. How can it show 97.3% uptime?
narration.script: Fair challenge, and it comes down to how the cell's states were classified. Our formula is runtime over runtime plus downtime, so 97.3% says the equipment almost never faulted while it was running work. In OEE terms starved time is an availability loss, and uptime alone can't separate starvation from a slow cycle. The conclusion still holds, because a healthy machine missing plan by half is limited by something other than the machine, and the fishbone found it in kitting and an inflated target. The fix I'd make is putting starved time and cycle time against the design rate on the dashboard.

narration.script: As proof that it lasts, you shouldn't yet, and I wrote it up as a pilot. What it does show is the mechanism. That metric is timestamped and behavioral, so it's hard to fake. To make it convincing I'd stagger the rollout to second shift as a comparison, keep measuring after the novelty wears off, and report the full distribution, not only the median.

cards.q: How can 1,809 JSON records become more than 31 GB?
cards.easy: Each record holds lists of tests, each test lists of measurements, each measurement lists of readings. Expanding all of it into a flat table multiplies the rows, and every row repeats all the parent information, so size grows with the product of the list lengths.
cards.deep: Expanding nested arrays in place (Power Query's expand to new rows) multiplies rows at each level: a record with $T$ tests, $M$ measurements per test, and $C$ readings per measurement becomes $T \cdot M \cdot C$ rows, and every row repeats every parent field (ids, timestamps, test names, limits). Size scales roughly as $\text{records} \times T \times M \times C \times \text{row width}$, so moderate list lengths compound quickly. Expanding two sibling arrays from the same parent independently makes a cross product of unrelated lists, which is both larger and wrong. Untyped text columns make it worse, because Power BI's columnar engine compresses typed, low cardinality columns well and long JSON strings badly, and here the expansion was repeated on every visual. The cure has three parts: pick the output grain deliberately (one row per test event), walk the nesting along one explicit record path per output table so no accidental cross product happens, and cast types before load. The write up gives the inputs (809 and 1,000 records) and the result (more than 31 GB); know the actual list lengths from the data.

cards.q: Sketch the json_normalize and type casting code for records that nest tests, measurements, and readings.
cards.easy: One explicit record path per table you want, parent fields carried down as meta, then explicit type conversion and a computed cycle time column, written out with openpyxl.
cards.deep:
Illustrative sketch with placeholder field names (the real schema is in the project files):

```python
import json
import pandas as pd

with open("test_reports.json") as f:
    events = json.load(f)                      # list of test event records

# Event grain: one row per test event; nested lists stay out of this table
ev = pd.json_normalize(events, max_level=1)
ev = ev[["event_id", "station", "start_time", "end_time", "result"]]

# Reading grain, only if a drill down needs it: walk ONE path explicitly
readings = pd.json_normalize(
    events,
    record_path=["tests", "measurements", "readings"],
    meta=["event_id", ["tests", "name"]],
    record_prefix="reading.",
)

# Type contract, so Power Query never guesses
ev["start_time"] = pd.to_datetime(ev["start_time"], errors="raise")
ev["end_time"] = pd.to_datetime(ev["end_time"], errors="raise")
ev["passed"] = ev["result"].map({"PASS": True, "FAIL": False}).astype("boolean")
ev["cycle_time_s"] = (ev["end_time"] - ev["start_time"]).dt.total_seconds()
readings["reading.value"] = pd.to_numeric(readings["reading.value"], errors="raise")

with pd.ExcelWriter("jumper2_events.xlsx", engine="openpyxl") as xw:
    ev.to_excel(xw, sheet_name="events", index=False)
```

Design points: `record_path` names the list that becomes rows; `meta` carries parent fields down (nested ones as lists); one explicit path per output table prevents a cross product of sibling arrays. Mapping pass and fail into a nullable boolean leaves any unmapped value as `<NA>`, which a check can catch; `errors="raise"` makes a bad timestamp or reading fail loudly. The assertions Tanay says were missing would sit right after this: `ev["event_id"].is_unique`, no null timestamps, `(ev["cycle_time_s"] > 0).all()`, no `<NA>` in `passed`, and `len(ev) == len(events)`.

cards.q: What is an RF jumper cable, and what do continuity, return loss, and torque mean in its testing?
cards.easy: A jumper is a short radio frequency cable connecting a transmitter to an antenna. Continuity checks the conductors are connected, return loss measures how much signal bounces back at the connectors, and torque is how tightly each connector is fastened.
cards.deep: Jumpers are short coaxial assemblies terminated with RF connectors; the write up calls them functionally simple and precision sensitive, with every connector terminated to tight torque and electrical specification. Continuity: center conductor and shield are each continuous and not shorted to each other. Return loss: incident over reflected power at the port, $\text{RL} = 10\log_{10}(P_{inc}/P_{ref}) = -20\log_{10}|\Gamma|$ dB, where $\Gamma$ is the reflection coefficient; higher is better, and any impedance discontinuity (a poorly seated connector, a deformed dielectric, a bad termination) reflects power and lowers it. Torque: connectors are tightened to a specified torque; too little leaves an unstable contact and too much deforms parts, and either can surface as a return loss failure, so torque and return loss plausibly share causes. Visual inspection catches assembly and cosmetic defects. Passing all three on the first attempt is what counts as good for First Time Throughput.

cards.q: What is the theory of constraints, and how does it apply here?
cards.easy: The theory of constraints says every system's output is limited by one bottleneck, and improving anything else does not raise output. Here the bottleneck was the material feed into the automated cell, while the cell itself had spare capacity.
cards.deep: Goldratt (The Goal, 1984): the whole system's throughput is set by its constraint, and only increasing flow through the constraint raises throughput. Five focusing steps: identify the constraint; exploit it (get the most from it without spending, for example never letting it starve); subordinate everything else to that decision; raise its capacity if it still binds (the investment step); then return to step one without letting inertia become the new constraint. Drum buffer rope schedules to the constraint's pace (drum), protects it with a time buffer of work in front of it (buffer), and releases material only as the constraint consumes it (rope). Constraint types: equipment, people, policy. Applied: identify, 97.3% uptime with 46.3% attainment says the cell is not the constraint and the kitting feed is; exploit and subordinate, a two bin continuous feed is a buffer in front of the cell, and kitting batches sized for the manual line are a policy constraint (a rule, not a machine). Only after that would added capacity make sense. Policy and method constraints are typical and cheap to fix.

cards.q: What is a Pugh matrix, and what are its weaknesses?
cards.easy: A Pugh matrix compares several options against one reference option, criterion by criterion, marking each as better, the same, or worse. It is a quick, transparent way to pick among candidates.
cards.deep: Setup: choose criteria (for an engagement like this, plausible ones are impact on schedule attainment, cost, implementation time, operator burden, and sustainability; the real list is in the project files), choose a reference candidate (the datum, often the current state), and score each other candidate as better (+1), same (0), or worse (-1) on each criterion; the weighted variant multiplies by criterion weights. Read the counts of better and worse, then strengthen the leading candidate by borrowing strengths from others and iterate. Strengths: forces explicit criteria, fast, works in a room with stakeholders. Weaknesses: the criteria list is arbitrary and may be incomplete; several minor criteria can outvote a must have; the scores are ordinal judgments that look more quantitative than they are; and the result depends on which reference was chosen. A defensible use fixes criteria and weights in advance, treats must haves as gates, and checks the winner survives a change of reference.

cards.q: What is a two bin continuous kitting feed, and why does it fix starvation?

cards.deep: Two bin is the simplest kanban: a visual pull signal in which consumption, rather than a forecast or a large batch schedule, triggers replenishment. Why it fits: kitting batches sized for the manual line delivered material to the automated cell in lumps, so the cell alternated between running and waiting; small, continuous replenishment matches the cell's consumption. Risks: bins sized too small starve the cell anyway, the kitting area must respond within the lead time, and connector subassemblies arriving batched from upstream would also have to change, since the fishbone flagged them.

cards.q: What is an FMEA, and what does one look like for a dashboard?
cards.easy: Failure Mode and Effects Analysis lists every way something can fail, what happens when it does, and how likely and how detectable each failure is, then ranks them so the worst get fixed first.
cards.deep: For each function, list failure modes, effects, and causes; score Severity, Occurrence, and Detection on ordinal scales (a higher Detection score means harder to detect); rank by Risk Priority Number $\text{RPN} = S \times O \times D$ and act on the highest first. Illustrative rows for a KPI dashboard (the real rows are in the project's Control Plan): refresh fails silently and shows last week's numbers (high severity, poor detectability; mitigate with a visible data as of timestamp and an owner check); an upstream PLC schema change makes a measure return zeros or blanks (mitigate with validation assertions in the pipeline, the missing unit tests); a target changes in the document but not in the measure; a slicer left on hides one line. Criticisms: multiplying ordinal scores treats them as ratio data, different combinations can rank in surprising orders, and the 2019 AIAG and VDA handbook replaced RPN with Action Priority for that reason.

Revalidating the manual target belongs in the same loop the team ran for the cell, once kitting flows continuously and the manual line no longer has to compensate; resetting it during the shortfall would bake the compensation into the plan. Also check the uptime denominator on a manual line: scheduled hours across two ten hour shifts versus hours with operators assigned.

We fixed the automated cell's target first because that one was keeping the dashboard permanently red. The manual line's target should go through the same revalidation once kitting stops forcing it to compensate.

cards.q: This is a Power BI dashboard and a spreadsheet pipeline. Why is it relevant to an ML or data engineering role?
cards.easy: The hard parts are the same ones: turning messy nested machine data into a typed table at the right grain, getting agreement on what a metric means, and reaching the conclusion the data supports instead of the one people expected.

Defend: the pipeline problem (three levels of nested arrays in event JSON, choosing the grain, explicit record paths, a type contract so the consumer never coerces) is the same problem as building features or warehouse tables from event data; the definition work is metric design, which is what an ML evaluation spec or an analytics engineering semantic layer is; the finding is a diagnosis from two metrics that contradicted the floor's belief; and the engagement shows judgment with senior stakeholders, a measured pilot, and a projection labelled as a projection. The gaps Tanay states plainly (no unit tests, no culture baseline) reflect the same discipline expected in production data work.

cards.q: What are the limits of what was delivered, what breaks at 10x, and what would come next?
cards.easy: The pipeline is an untested script that writes a workbook, which is fine for two datasets and one dashboard but not for many lines or plants. Next would be tests, scheduled loads into a proper database, and following through on the kitting change and the culture baseline.
cards.deep: Limits: a Python script without tests, run on demand, writing an Excel workbook; definitions live in a document and in DAX measures with no single governed metric layer; Culture and Engagement has no baseline; the pilot was two weeks on one shift; the $355,000 is a projection. At 10x (ten lines or several plants, continuous PLC feeds): workbooks stop working as the interface, so land flattened events in a database or warehouse table partitioned by date and line, load incrementally keyed on test event id, validate the schema at ingest so an upstream change fails loudly, and schedule refreshes with an orchestrator. Keep the KPI formulas in one governed layer (dbt models or a shared Power BI semantic model) so every plant computes Uptime the same way, which is the original problem at larger scale. Business next steps: implement two bin kitting and track attainment against the ramp of about 200 cables a week, run the first culture survey for a baseline, roll the standup to second shift as a staggered comparison, and get JMA Finance to confirm or replace the two rates.
